criteria: Price above both the mid and slow moving averages
Mid moving average above the slow one
Fast moving average above both mid and slow
Price above the fast moving average

evidence.headline: Backtesting could not establish that a Minervini pass predicts anything on this market.
detail: On daily bars, stocks passing the template returned 1.21% over the next 20 trading days against 2.68% for those that did not — a gap of -1.5 points, in the opposite direction to the textbook reading. Weekly is -1.0; monthly is +0.2.

That average is one episode, not a pattern. The daily gap was positive in only 2 of 7 two-month periods, but it ranges from -8.9 to +3.0, and the single worst period (Jan-Feb 2026) drags the average from -0.5 to -1.7 on its own. Drop that one period and daily is -0.5, weekly +0.2 and monthly +1.6 — all indistinguishable from nothing.

The three timeframes do not agree. Monthly is positive in 5 of 7 periods and carries the opposite sign to daily and weekly, which is what disagreement between noisy measurements of no effect looks like.

Fitting the direction on a training period and testing it out-of-sample gave a different answer depending on where the split was drawn: two split dates confirmed an inverted signal, the most recent one reversed it on all three timeframes.

Monthly bars use 2/7/10-bar averages as a calendar stand-in for 50/150/200 days. A full-length monthly template needs about 31 monthly bars and only 4 of 391 stocks have that, so monthly is indicative only.
evidence.verdict: Treat a pass as a description of where the stock currently sits in its trend, not as a prediction. Nothing here supports trading it in either direction.

method.measures: For every bar the template can be fully evaluated on, the forward return over that timeframe's horizon is recorded. "Spread" is the mean forward return of passing bars minus the mean of non-passing bars, in percentage points. A positive spread means passing stocks went on to do better.
method.lookahead: None. Every moving average, 52-week extreme and criterion is computed from bars at or before the evaluated bar, by the same engine the live page uses.
method.noTradePlan: The Trend Template is a state, not a trade. There is no entry, stoploss or target to hit, so this backtest measures forward returns rather than win rates on simulated positions.
method.unresolved: Bars with no forward data — the tail of every price file — are dropped rather than counted as flat, so the most recent bars cannot inflate the sample.
method.monthlyCaveat: Monthly uses 2/7/10-bar averages as a calendar-equivalent of 50/150/200 days. A full-length monthly template needs ~31 monthly bars and only a handful of stocks have that, so monthly rests on ~13 evaluable bars per stock and is indicative only.
method.crossModel: Each period also carries the Super Model's ranking edge for the same two months, read from data/super-model-backtest.json. The two are not independent: the Super Model scores a Minervini pass negatively, so a period where passing stocks slumped is by construction a period where it ranks well. Both results lean on the same episode.
method.overlap: Observations overlap: consecutive bars share most of their forward window, so the observation count is much larger than the number of independent episodes. Treat the period-by-period distribution, not the observation count, as the measure of how much evidence there is.

caveats: The universe only has usable price history from around May 2025. Everything before that comes from a handful of stocks — read this as roughly a 14-month test, not a decade.
One two-month period (Jan-Feb 2026) accounts for most of the negative result on all three timeframes. Excluding it, every timeframe sits within half a point of zero.

That same period is the Super Model's single best stretch (+12.9 ranking edge). The two are not independent — the Super Model scores a Minervini pass negatively, so an episode where passing stocks slumped is by construction one where it ranks well. Both results lean on the same episode.

Observations overlap heavily: consecutive bars share most of their forward window, so tens of thousands of observations represent far fewer independent episodes. The period-by-period spread, not the observation count, is the measure of how much evidence there is.

At longer horizons every timeframe turns more negative (daily -2.9 over 60 bars, weekly -4.4 over 13, monthly -3.1 over 3). This is reported rather than dropped, but it rests on the same short history.
Nothing here is a trade. The Trend Template is a state, not an entry — there is no stoploss or target being tested, so a "spread" is not a return you could have earned.
